titulo: Two words, then a smaller question
subtitulo: The answer arrives long; you make it short enough to walk on
introPt: A corner in the centre, a stranger stopped mid-stride, and an answer with more streets in it than you can hold. Listen right to the end.
cenario: Central Athens, late afternoon. A traveller with a dead phone stops a woman on the pavement to find the port bus.

dialogo.pt: Excuse me, where is the bus stop?

dialogo.es: Ευθεία, μετά την εκκλησία δεξιά, και είναι απέναντι από το περίπτερο.
dialogo.pt: Straight on, right after the church, and it's opposite the kiosk.
dialogo.tts: Ευθεία, μετά την εκκλησία δεξιά, και είναι απέναντι από το περίπτερο.

dialogo.es: Όχι, πέντε λεπτά με τα πόδια. Ελάτε, σας δείχνω.
dialogo.pt: No, five minutes on foot. Come on, I'll show you.
dialogo.tts: Όχι, πέντε λεπτά με τα πόδια. Ελάτε, σας δείχνω.

perguntas.pergunta: The second question is the useful one. What makes Είναι μακριά; work so well?
opcoes: It is more polite than the first question
Its answer is a yes, a no or a number — something you can hold and act on
It signals that you speak fluent Greek
It obliges the other person to walk you there
perguntas.explica: Πού είναι opens the door and can bring back a paragraph. The follow-up is built so the answer fits in your head: far or not far, left or right, five minutes.

perguntas.pergunta: The stranger ended with Ελάτε, σας δείχνω — come on, I'll show you. How should that be read?
opcoes: As an unusually forward gesture that calls for polite refusal
As a hint that the directions were too complicated for a foreigner
As the ordinary local shape of helpfulness, described in research as an orientation to closeness
As the opening of a paid guiding service
perguntas.explica: Comparative work on the two languages describes Greek politeness as oriented to involvement and English to distance. Taking charge of your problem is what helping looks like here — it is not a reading of your competence.

perguntas.pergunta: What goes into the hole after Πού είναι?
opcoes: The place, in the dictionary form you see on the map
The place, with an ending changed to mark the object
A verb saying what you want to do there
Your own position first, then the place
perguntas.explica: This frame deliberately takes the place in its plain form. You recognise the word on a sign or a map and you say it unchanged — which is what makes it usable while you are still decoding the alphabet.

perguntas.pergunta: A road sign reads ΡΟΔΟΣ and, underneath, RODOS. You want to say it out loud. What do you do?
opcoes: Read the Latin line, since it was written for visitors
Read the Greek line: that Ρ is an R, and the Latin line maps letters, not sounds
Avoid the name and point at the sign instead
Say it as Podos, since Ρ looks like P
perguntas.explica: The place-name authority notes that the romanisation on Greek signs is a less reliable guide to pronunciation than the system it replaced. Use the Latin line to identify the place and the Greek one to say it.

perguntas.pergunta: Which reply tells you to keep walking without giving you a single street name?
opcoes: Απέναντι από το περίπτερο
Μετά την εκκλησία δεξιά
Πέντε λεπτά με τα πόδια
Ευθεία
perguntas.explica: Πέντε λεπτά με τα πόδια is a complete, actionable answer with no navigation in it at all. Ten words like this one — κοντά, μακριά, δίπλα, απέναντι — cover most of what comes back.
